papers.title: Polynomial-Time Computation of Extensive-Form Proper Equilibria in Two-Player Zero-Sum Games
papers.abstract: We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for computing an exact extensive-form proper equilibrium in a finite two-player zero-sum extensive-form game with perfect recall and rational data. Properness is understood in the agent normal form: an action at an information set is penalized relative to a better action while all other local behavioral choices, including the player's own future actions, remain fixed. Our algorithm assigns each information set a geometric permutahedron of allowable action probabilities. A scaled doubly stochastic representation embeds these restrictions in a polynomial-size sequence-form polytope; a saddle point then satisfies the local $\varepsilon$-properness inequalities. To obtain an exact equilibrium rather than a solution at an arbitrarily small numerical perturbation, we establish sign stability of a parametric linear system, construct a persistent feasible basis, and extract the limits of behavioral ratios. The resulting probabilities are rational and have polynomial encoding length, including at information sets whose realization probabilities vanish.

papers.title: Transparency in Team Contracts
papers.abstract: In contract design, the principal is often better informed about the project's chances of succeeding than the agents. To incentivize effort, the principal has two main tools: first, to design a contract, sharing part of the project's success among the agents; second, to design a (Bayesian) persuasion scheme, selectively sharing information with the agents. In this work we are interested in the optimal combination of both these tools. We tackle the joint problem through the prism of simplicity vs. optimality, and establish a stark dichotomy: The simple disclosure scheme of full transparency achieves a tight $4/3$-approximation to the optimal combination of information disclosure and team contract, when the team's production function is submodular. In contrast, full transparency can be arbitrarily far from optimal when production is supermodular. The techniques that we develop to bound the gap for submodular functions, also yield a new deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm for pure multi-agent contract design, with a significantly improved approximation ratio of $2.311$, and thus a $3.081$-approximation algorithm for the joint information and contracting problem.

papers.title: Cores of $3$-distant convex games
papers.abstract: Convex cooperative games have a nonempty core and admit an efficient construction of core allocations. However, economically natural local frictions may violate convexity. We study the core of $3$-distant convex games, which permit violations of convexity only between closely related coalitions. Although the core of such a game may be empty, we establish a simple necessary and sufficient condition for its nonemptiness. We also develop a strongly polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm for finding a core allocation whenever one exists. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of the framework to oligopolistic competition with merger synergies and profit allocation of joint production with complementary inputs.

papers.title: The w-value: Market Implementation and gamma-Core Stability in Pollution-Control Games
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel solution concept, called the w-value, for cooperative pollution-control games. The w-value is axiomatically founded on three principles: Pareto Optimality (PO), Market Equilibrium (ME), and Fiscal Balance (FB), which together yield an efficient and implementable welfare distribution. We establish its existence and uniqueness under standard concavity and convexity assumptions, and provide a market mechanism that implements it through price constraints and an initial permit allocation. A key theoretical advantage is its strong stability: the w-value belongs to the gamma-core, which makes it resistant to coalitional deviations. Moreover, the w-value can be obtained through a simple step-by-step procedure, which facilitates its application to complex real-world problems. A numerical illustration demonstrates the step-by-step calculation process and confirms the gamma-core membership numerically. Finally, we apply the concept to international climate negotiations, showing how it provides a theoretical rationale for the shift from rigid mandatory emission reduction systems toward the flexible structure of Nationally Determined Contributions.

papers.title: Robust Mechanism Design with Anonymous Information
papers.abstract: In practice, auction data are often endogenously censored and anonymous, revealing only limited outcome statistics rather than full bid profiles. We study robust auction design when the seller observes only the distribution of a single anonymous order statistic of the bidders' values and seeks to maximize worst-case expected revenue over all product distributions consistent with the observed statistic. We show that simple and widely used mechanisms are robustly optimal. Specifically, posted pricing is robustly optimal given the distribution of the highest value; the Myerson auction designed for the unique consistent i.i.d. distribution, with uniformly random tie-breaking, is robustly optimal given the lowest value distribution; and the second-price auction with an optimal reserve is robustly optimal when an intermediate order statistic is observed and the implied i.i.d. distribution is regular above its reserve. Without any regularity assumption, when the second-highest value is observed, the best worst-case revenue of a second-price auction with a reserve is still at least a $2-\sqrt{2}\approx 0.586$ fraction of the optimal worst-case revenue. More generally, for a broad class of monotone symmetric mechanisms depending only on the top $k$ order statistics, including multi-unit and position auctions, the worst-case revenue is attained under the i.i.d. distribution consistent with the observed $k$-th order statistic. Our results provide a tractable foundation for non-discriminatory auction design, where fairness and privacy are intrinsic consequences of the information structure rather than imposed constraints.

papers.title: Cohesion-Sensitive Power Indices: Representation Results for Banzhaf and Shapley Values
papers.abstract: In many applications of cooperative game theory -- from corporate governance and cartel formation to parliamentary voting -- not all winning coalitions are feasible. Ideological distances, institutional constraints, or pre-electoral agreements may render certain coalitions implausible. Classical power indices ignore this and weight all winning coalitions equally. We introduce cohesion structures to quantify coalition feasibility and axiomatically characterize two families of cohesion-sensitive power indices, represented as expected marginal contributions under Luce-type distributions. In the Banzhaf branch, coalition weights are a power transformation of cohesion; in the Shapley branch, additional axioms separate size from cohesion, recovering the classical size weights with cohesion acting within each size class. All results have been mechanically verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib. We illustrate the framework on the German Bundestag and the French Assembl\'ee Nationale, where cordon sanitaire and double cordon scenarios produce sharp, interpretable power shifts.

papers.title: Complex Menus in Discriminatory Pricing
papers.abstract: Advances in technology decrease the costs of offering and choosing from large menus of varieties. As these complexity costs fall, how large are the menus offered by monopolists likely to become? For the multi-product or multi-attribute case, ubiquitous in practice, we show that optimal menus are generically infinite in the absence of complexity costs. Complexity costs can decrease the menu size, but it grows without bound as these costs decrease. These results have no analogue in the single-dimensional model and do not rely on non-linearities in production costs or preferences; the extensive product differentiation is caused by screening considerations alone.

papers.title: Brave New Data: Pricing Expertise and Discovery
papers.abstract: We study the procurement of verifiable evidence from an expert who privately assesses a binary state and chooses the direction and intensity of evidence acquisition. The buyer balances the ease of inducing discovery against its value for decisions beyond the expert's initial assessment. An optimal contract pays only for disclosed evidence, independently of the initial report. When acquisition is cheap, equal rewards for evidence of either state induce intensive search whose failure is informative. As costs rise, rewarding evidence of only one state becomes optimal despite the symmetry of the environment, reducing expected payments at the expense of decision accuracy.

papers.title: Robust prizes in all-pay contests with loss aversion
papers.abstract: We study robust prize design in all-pay contests with loss-averse agents when the principal does not know the agents' convex cost of effort, subject to an aggregate productivity constraint. The robustly optimal prize structure awards equal prizes to all contestants except the one ranked last. The optimal bottom prize is zero under moderate loss aversion, but becomes positive and increases with loss aversion when loss aversion is sufficiently strong. Under strong loss aversion, the robust solution involves partial participation in the contest.

papers.title: Designing Public Information for Strategic Advice
papers.abstract: A principal chooses an action using advice from an expert who privately knows local conditions. Before receiving advice, she can commission a public study of an independent state, such as future demand, that changes the expected conflict between their preferred actions. We show that the communication protocol determines the optimal study. Under optimal mediation, the value of advice is convex in conflict, making full revelation optimal. Under commitment to an action rule, the principal may prefer no information, while informative optimal studies include a report certifying high conflict. Under unmediated cheap talk, changes in the number of equilibrium messages create upward kinks in the value of advice. Optimal studies avoid interior communication thresholds and can induce two distant communication regimes while skipping every regime in between, strictly outperforming both full revelation and no information. When the principal retains the raw data, selective public disclosure can improve advice without sacrificing forecasting precision. We discuss implications for fiscal forecasts and spending agencies.

papers.title: Unobserved Consideration and Consumer Welfare
papers.abstract: Can welfare effects of price change be identified when consumers' consideration sets are heterogeneous and unobserved? We establish that the welfare distribution is the same functional of structural choice probabilities under stable but limited consideration as under full consideration. The result permits unrestricted income-effects, preference heterogeneity, and dependence between preferences and consideration. Within this class, limited consideration admits a full-consideration representation preserving choice-probabilities and money-metric compensation: consideration/preferences can remain unidentified while demand and welfare are identified. When consideration sets contract as prices rise, the welfare distribution can be bounded using demand and a bound on choice-set attrition.

papers.title: Discrete Choice under Congestion: Equilibrium and Welfare
papers.abstract: In many choice settings, a rise in aggregate demand for an option lowers an individual's payoff from choosing it. Driving becomes less attractive than taking a train when more commuters drive, clogging the highway. In such cases, a targeted intervention that mitigates the externality at the congested option can divert it elsewhere and also undermine preference based sorting, making overall welfare effects theoretically ambiguous. We develop an empirical framework to analyze such scenarios of endogenous congestion. We show that in these settings, equilibrium exists and is unique without restrictions on functional-form of utilities or dimension/distribution of preference heterogeneity, and even when congestion at one option affects payoffs from other choices. Under a linear-index structure, micro-data on choice enables semiparametric identification of utility contrasts and welfare effects of some, but not all, interventions. We apply the framework to Cambridge undergraduate admissions, where candidates apply through one constituent college, and admission probability depends on application numbers relative to capacity in that college. Using administrative micro-data on 25,325 applicants, we calculate welfare under two counterfactuals: (i) centralized random allocation and (ii) higher rent at popular colleges. Random allocation reduces welfare for everyone: it removes individual choice without improving admission chances since, by design, lower congestion at a college exactly counterbalances the lower probability of being allocated there. Targeted rent increase produces both gains and losses, with median loss for men and median gain for women. This exercise shows how identified preferences and equilibrium feedback jointly determine welfare when choices entail externalities.

papers.title: The Impact of Connectivity on the Production and Diffusion of Knowledge
papers.abstract: We study a social bandit problem featuring the production and diffusion of knowledge. While higher connectivity enhances knowledge diffusion, it may reduce knowledge production as agents shy away from experimentation and free-ride on others' discoveries. In the symmetric mixed-strategy equilibrium, exploration probability falls with connectivity, while expected per-capita equilibrium surplus is constant in the interior mixing region. Under finite-player pure strategies, surplus can fall discontinuously when the integer number of explorers drops. In the large-population limit these jumps vanish, and per-capita equilibrium surplus is weakly increasing in connectivity and eventually flat for intermediate beliefs.

papers.title: Optimal Large-Contest Design
papers.abstract: In this paper, we provide a theoretical framework to analyze the optimal design of large contests, such as university admissions and research funding. Under a broad class of distributional preferences, the optimal allocation rules are step functions with at most two steps, thus rationalizing several real-world examples. From a methodological perspective, we leverage the mathematics of extreme points to characterize optimal allocation rules in environments where the distribution of efforts can be endogenous. When the designer wants to maximize aggregate effort, the optimal allocation rule sets a performance threshold and it awards prizes at random above it, provided noise is sufficiently small. When noise is larger, awarding prizes to the best performers becomes optimal.

papers.title: Timing, Entry, and Revenue in Clock-Based Platform Markets
papers.abstract: On platforms where time-to-contract is itself payoff-relevant--Aalsmeer's flower auctions, ride-hailing dispatch, on-demand-labor matching--the textbook revenue equivalence between Dutch and first-price formats holds the trading outcome fixed. Once participation is endogenous and both sides bear waiting costs, the trading format directly shapes who enters, market thickness, volume, and platform revenue. The platform's ranking of the descending clock against immediate and batched posted-price benchmarks is decided by two estimable primitives on each side of the market: an earnings gap and a timing gap. A bidirectional four-case classification identifies when the descending clock dominates at every level of waiting costs, only above a floor, only below a ceiling, or not at all; the last case is unconditional -- when the descending clock charges no more per trade and contracts no faster than the posted-price benchmark, it cannot win. No format admits a universal ranking. The local verdict propagates through endogenous entry, and cross-side complementarity amplifies shared local advantages into joint dominance. A conditional revenue theorem converts entry and volume gains into a platform-revenue ranking. In calibrated parameterizations the revenue-ranking switching boundary lies near $p_0/\bar v\approx 1$, inside the empirical range for ride-hailing platforms. A measurement protocol provides explicit nonparametric estimators for the six reduced-form objects and a test statistic for the dominance condition, and a Lean~4 formalization audits the algebraic and order-theoretic content. In markets where goods or services cannot wait, the speed of the trading mechanism is a primitive of market design.

papers.title: Resource Allocation with Midterm Review
papers.abstract: A principal funds an agent's project over two periods, with a midterm review providing a public signal about project quality. The agent privately knows the project's quality and always prefers more funding, while the principal wants to match funding to quality. We show that the optimal mechanism frontloads the review's information value: the principal's expected payoff is strictly higher in the first period than in the second, even though she is better informed after the review. In the optimal mechanism, higher-quality projects receive more funding initially but face larger cuts after a bad review, leaving them with less funding than lower-quality projects. A good review increases funding, but the resulting allocation does not preserve the initial ranking of projects and, under a mild condition, declines with quality near the top.
